rh-l4q2.summary: Holcot asks whether confirmation is a sacrament, and in a brief, largely canonistic question answers yes. Its substance includes chrism as matter, a Trinitarian signing as form, an episcopal minister with right intention, and a willing baptized recipient. Christ instituted it when laying hands on children, though its rite was concealed in the early Church. It is necessary for the well-being of a Christian rather than for salvation itself, and it is ordinarily episcopal but delegable to priests.
claims: Confirmation is a sacrament instituted by Christ.
It is necessary for well-being, not salvation.

rh-l4q2-Dd1e103.summary: Opening statement: whether confirmation is a sacrament.

rh-l4q2-d1e105.summary: States the question: whether confirmation is a sacrament.

rh-l4q2-Dd1e115.summary: Arguments against confirmation's sacramentality: no Gospel institution, no apostolic form or matter, it would then be necessary for salvation, any confirmed person could confirm, and degraded bishops could confirm. Canon law is cited for the opposite.
claims: Confirmation's sacramental status is questioned on grounds of institution, form, and necessity.

rh-l4q2-d1e117.summary: First argument against: every sacrament was instituted by Christ, but confirmation is not read of in the Gospel.
claims: Confirmation's institution by Christ is not recorded in the Gospel.

rh-l4q2-d1e130.summary: Further: a sacrament has definite form and matter, but the apostles used no form and no matter, confirming by laying on of hands alone (Acts 8).
claims: The apostles confirmed without form or matter.

rh-l4q2-d1e146.summary: Further: it would be a sacrament of necessity, since Pope Urban (De consecratione d. 5) says all the faithful must receive the Spirit by episcopal imposition of hands after baptism to be full Christians, and being a full Christian is necessary for salvation.
claims: Confirmation would be necessary for salvation.

rh-l4q2-d1e168.summary: Further: anyone confirmed could confirm, having the character of confirmation and so able to cause a like one.
claims: The confirmed could confer confirmation.

rh-l4q2-d1e177.summary: Further: a degraded bishop could confirm and consecrate, since the character is indelible.
claims: A degraded bishop could still confirm.

rh-l4q2-d1e189.summary: For the opposite: De consecratione d. 5 throughout.
claims: Canon law treats confirmation as a sacrament.

rh-l4q2-Dd1e195.summary: Holcot affirms that confirmation is a sacrament and lists its six substantial requirements: chrism as matter, a Trinitarian signing as form, a bishop with due intention, and a willing baptized recipient.
claims: Confirmation is a sacrament with chrism as matter and a Trinitarian form.

rh-l4q2-d1e200.summary: Answer: yes. Six things belong to its substance: matter and form; on the minister's side episcopal dignity and due intention; on the recipient's, devotion or will and prior baptism, the gate of sacraments. The matter is chrism, olive oil mixed with balsam consecrated by a bishop; the form 'I sign you with the sign of the cross and confirm you with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father...'.
claims: Confirmation is a sacrament.
Its matter is episcopally consecrated chrism and its form a Trinitarian signing.
It requires a bishop, due intention, the recipient's will, and baptism.

rh-l4q2-Dd1e235.summary: Christ instituted confirmation by laying hands on children, and its rite was hidden in the early Church to avoid pagan mockery. It is necessary for well-being, not for salvation. Bishops ordinarily confer it but may delegate priests. A degraded bishop remains a bishop. Practical notes on the rite follow.
claims: Christ instituted confirmation.
Confirmation is necessary for well-being, not salvation.

rh-l4q2-d1e240.summary: Reply to the first: Christ instituted it when he laid hands on children (Matthew 19). Form and matter are not recorded, since matters not necessary for salvation were hidden in the early Church because of pagan mockery, as Dionysius excuses himself from detailing sacramental rites.
claims: Christ instituted confirmation by laying hands on children.
Sacramental rites were concealed in the early Church.

rh-l4q2-d1e264.summary: Reply to the second: the apostles used some form though it was not written.
claims: The apostles used an unwritten form.

rh-l4q2-d1e271.summary: Reply to the third: it is necessary not for being but for well-being.
claims: Confirmation is necessary for well-being, not for salvation simply.

rh-l4q2-d1e278.summary: Reply to the fourth: commonly only bishops can confer it, though it can be committed to a simple priest (De consecratione d. 5, gloss).
claims: Bishops ordinarily confirm, but priests may be delegated.

rh-l4q2-d1e288.summary: Reply to the fifth: some say yes, since a degraded bishop remains a bishop. Notes: one must receive confirmation because it strengthens and signifies need of strength; sponsors may be of either sex; the anointed places should be bound with cloth until dry; and the confirmed should keep discipline for seven days for the sevenfold grace of the Spirit.
claims: A degraded bishop remains a bishop.
Confirmation strengthens the recipient.
